text.title: The Shepherd
text.author: Katherine Mansfield
text.description: A pastoral scene of early morning in Crescent Bay where an old shepherd, his dog Wag, and a flock of sheep move through the misty landscape as the sun rises, passing by the summer colony and heading toward Daylight Cove.

rootSpan.title: The Shepherd
rootSpan.description: A pastoral scene of early morning in Crescent Bay where an old shepherd, his dog Wag, and a flock of sheep move through the misty landscape as the sun rises, passing by the summer colony and heading toward Daylight Cove.

childSpans.title: Dawn in the Mist
childSpans.description: The opening of the story establishing the early morning setting of Crescent Bay shrouded in white mist and dew.

childSpans.title: Landscape Obscured by Mist
childSpans.description: Description of Crescent Bay hidden under white sea-mist with dew-covered vegetation and indistinct boundaries between land and sea.

childSpans.title: The Shepherd's Arrival
childSpans.description: The shepherd, his dog, and flock of sheep appear and begin moving through the landscape.

childSpans.title: Flock Rounds the Corner
childSpans.description: The sheep and shepherd come into view from around the corner of Crescent Bay, moving along the sandy road.

childSpans.title: The Sun Rises
childSpans.description: The mist dissolves as the sun rises, revealing the landscape in bright light.

childSpans.title: Passing the Summer Colony
childSpans.description: The shepherd and flock pass by the sleeping summer colony and encounter Florrie the cat before heading toward Daylight Cove.

childSpans.title: The Sleeping Colony
childSpans.description: The sheep's bleating reaches the ears of sleeping inhabitants and children in the summer colony.

childSpans.title: Departure Toward Daylight Cove
childSpans.description: The shepherd and flock continue on, passing the fisherman's hut and milk-girl's dwelling, heading toward the rocky pass and Daylight Cove.

childSpans.title: Stanley's Arrival and Entry
childSpans.description: Stanley Burnell exits a bungalow and races to the sea for his morning bathe

childSpans.title: Stanley Rushes to the Beach
childSpans.description: Stanley bursts from the bungalow and races across the paddock and beach toward the sea

childSpans.title: Stanley Emerges from Bungalow
childSpans.description: Stanley in broad-striped bathing suit flings from the back door

childSpans.title: Stanley Races Across Landscape
childSpans.description: Stanley clears the stile, rushes through tussock grass, staggers up sandy hillock, races over stones and pebbles

childSpans.title: Stanley's Triumphant Entry
childSpans.description: Stanley wades into the water, believing himself first as usual

childSpans.title: Stanley Wades Out Exulting
childSpans.description: Stanley wades into the water, splashing, believing he is first man in

childSpans.title: Stanley Soused His Head
childSpans.description: Stanley swoops down to souse his head and neck in the water

childSpans.title: Jonathan Trout's Appearance
childSpans.description: Jonathan Trout's voice hails Stanley from the water, revealing he was already there

childSpans.title: Jonathan's Greeting
childSpans.description: Jonathan Trout's velvety bass voice booms across the water, startling Stanley

childSpans.title: Jonathan's Voice Booms
childSpans.description: A velvety bass voice hails Stanley from the water

childSpans.title: Stanley Discovers Jonathan
childSpans.description: Stanley lifts up to see Jonathan's dark head bobbing far out with arm lifted

childSpans.title: Jonathan Comments on Morning
childSpans.description: Jonathan sings about the glorious morning

childSpans.title: Stanley's Curt Response
childSpans.description: Stanley responds briefly and irritably to Jonathan's greeting

childSpans.title: Stanley's Brief Response
childSpans.description: Stanley says 'Yes, very fine!' briefly

childSpans.title: Stanley's Internal Irritation
childSpans.description: Stanley internally questions why Jonathan is in his spot and begins swimming

childSpans.title: The Conversation Conflict
childSpans.description: Jonathan attempts conversation about his dream while Stanley grows increasingly irritated and dismissive

childSpans.title: Jonathan's Dream
childSpans.description: Jonathan shouts about his extraordinary dream while Stanley swims and splashes to avoid conversation

childSpans.title: Jonathan Announces Dream
childSpans.description: Jonathan shouts about having an extraordinary dream last night

childSpans.title: Stanley's Splashing Avoidance
childSpans.description: Stanley turns on his back and kicks violently to avoid listening

childSpans.title: Jonathan Describes Cliff Dream
childSpans.description: Jonathan describes dreaming of hanging over a high cliff and shouting below

childSpans.title: Stanley's Dismissal
childSpans.description: Stanley tells Jonathan he has no time for conversation and must hurry

childSpans.title: Stanley Stops Splashing
childSpans.description: Stanley stops his violent splashing and addresses Jonathan directly

childSpans.title: Stanley States His Hurry
childSpans.description: Stanley tells Jonathan he is in rather a hurry this morning

childSpans.title: Jonathan's Surprise
childSpans.description: Jonathan is surprised or pretends to be, sinking under water then reappearing

childSpans.title: Stanley Explains His Hurry
childSpans.description: Stanley explains he has work to do this morning and no time to fool about

childSpans.title: Jonathan Departs
childSpans.description: Jonathan says 'Pass, friend!' and slides away through the water with scarcely a ripple

childSpans.title: Stanley's Departure
childSpans.description: Stanley rushes out of the water feeling cheated by the encounter

childSpans.title: Stanley Exits the Water
childSpans.description: Stanley curses Jonathan and rushes out of the water feeling his bathe is ruined

childSpans.title: Stanley Curses Jonathan
childSpans.description: Stanley internally curses Jonathan for ruining his bathe

childSpans.title: Stanley Swims Out Again
childSpans.description: Stanley strikes out to sea again, then quickly swims back in

childSpans.title: Stanley Rushes Up the Beach
childSpans.description: Stanley rushes away up the beach feeling cheated

childSpans.title: Jonathan's Reflection
childSpans.description: Jonathan remains in the water, reflecting on his feelings toward Stanley and his philosophy of life

childSpans.title: Jonathan's Philosophical Reflection
childSpans.description: Jonathan floats in the water, contemplating his relationship with Stanley and his life philosophy

childSpans.title: Jonathan Floats
childSpans.description: Jonathan floats gently, moving his hands like fins, letting the sea rock his body

childSpans.title: Jonathan Reflects on Stanley
childSpans.description: Jonathan reflects that despite his desire to tease Stanley, he is fond of him and feels sorry for his pathetic determination

childSpans.title: Jonathan Lifted by Wave
childSpans.description: An immense wave lifts Jonathan and breaks along the beach joyfully

childSpans.title: Jonathan's Life Philosophy
childSpans.description: Jonathan articulates his philosophy of living carelessly and recklessly, not fighting against life's ebb and flow

childSpans.title: Jonathan's Exit
childSpans.description: Jonathan exits the water, turning blue with cold and realizing his bathe is also spoiled

childSpans.title: Jonathan Exits the Water
childSpans.description: Jonathan exits the water, turning blue with cold and realizing he stayed in too long

childSpans.title: Jonathan Turns Blue with Cold
childSpans.description: Jonathan turns blue with cold, aching all over as though blood is being wrung from him

childSpans.title: Jonathan Wades to Shore
childSpans.description: Jonathan stalks up the beach shivering with tight muscles

childSpans.title: Jonathan Realizes Bathe Spoilt
childSpans.description: Jonathan realizes his bathe is spoilt because he stayed in too long

childSpans.title: Stanley's Breakfast and Departure
childSpans.description: Stanley arrives for breakfast, eats hastily, searches for his stick, and leaves for town

childSpans.title: Breakfast at the Table
childSpans.description: Stanley sits down to breakfast with Beryl and discusses his tight schedule

childSpans.title: Stanley's Arrival
childSpans.description: Stanley enters in his town suit and announces his time constraint

childSpans.title: The Forgotten Sugar
childSpans.description: Beryl forgets to add sugar to Stanley's tea, causing him concern

childSpans.title: Beryl's Evasion
childSpans.description: Stanley questions Beryl about her strange behavior; she deflects

childSpans.title: The Children and Mrs. Fairfield Arrive
childSpans.description: The three girls and Mrs. Fairfield bring porridge and join the table

childSpans.title: Children Enter with Porridge
childSpans.description: The three girls carefully carry porridge plates; Mrs. Fairfield follows with the tray

childSpans.title: Good Morning Exchange
childSpans.description: Mrs. Fairfield greets Stanley and reports on the boy; she gazes out at the garden

childSpans.title: Kezia's Porridge Play
childSpans.description: Beryl scolds Kezia for playing with her food; the children discuss eating habits

childSpans.title: Beryl's Complaint
childSpans.description: Beryl criticizes Kezia for digging a river in her porridge

childSpans.title: Children's Defense
childSpans.description: Kezia and the other girls defend their eating methods

childSpans.title: The Search for Stanley's Stick
childSpans.description: Stanley discovers his walking stick is missing and frantically searches for it

childSpans.title: Stanley Discovers the Stick is Missing
childSpans.description: Stanley realizes his stick is gone and demands it be found immediately

childSpans.title: Household Search
childSpans.description: Alice and others are drawn into searching for the stick

childSpans.title: Stanley Confronts Linda
childSpans.description: Stanley rushes to the bedroom to tell Linda about the missing stick

childSpans.title: Stanley's Departure
childSpans.description: Stanley leaves for town in the coach; Beryl calls from the gate

childSpans.title: The Coach Arrives
childSpans.description: Beryl calls from the gate that the coach has arrived; Stanley rushes out

childSpans.title: Beryl Calls from the Gate
childSpans.description: Beryl's voice cries out that the coach is waiting

childSpans.title: Stanley Departs
childSpans.description: Stanley grabs his hat and dashes out of the house

childSpans.title: Goodbye Exchange
childSpans.description: Stanley and Beryl exchange goodbyes; the coach departs

childSpans.title: The Household's Relief
childSpans.description: After Stanley's departure, the household experiences a palpable sense of freedom and joy

childSpans.title: Beryl Announces Stanley's Departure
childSpans.description: Beryl runs back to the house and announces that Stanley is gone

childSpans.title: Beryl's Announcement
childSpans.description: Beryl runs in and calls out that Stanley has gone

childSpans.title: Linda's Response
childSpans.description: Linda cries out from her room asking if Stanley has gone

childSpans.title: The Household Transforms
childSpans.description: The household experiences a dramatic shift in atmosphere and behavior

childSpans.title: Relief is Expressed
childSpans.description: The family acknowledges the relief of having the man out of the house

childSpans.title: Beryl's Celebration
childSpans.description: Beryl offers Mrs. Fairfield tea and expresses joy at their freedom

childSpans.title: Children Run Free
childSpans.description: The little girls run into the paddock like chickens let out of a coop

childSpans.title: Alice's Recklessness
childSpans.description: Even the servant girl Alice uses water recklessly and expresses disdain for men

childSpans.title: The Beach Expedition
childSpans.description: The children's journey to the beach and their interactions with other families.

childSpans.title: Crossing the Stile
childSpans.description: Lottie struggles to cross the stile while her sisters wait, and Kezia helps her over.

childSpans.title: Lottie's Struggle with the Stile
childSpans.description: Lottie finds it difficult to climb over the stile, her knees wobbling as she grasps the post.

childSpans.title: Isabel's Impatience
childSpans.description: Isabel urges Kezia to leave Lottie behind, offering her bucket as incentive.

childSpans.title: Kezia Helps Lottie
childSpans.description: Kezia returns to help Lottie cross the stile by instructing her on foot placement and sliding technique.

childSpans.title: Ascending the Hill
childSpans.description: The three girls climb the hill toward the beach, observing the Samuel Josephs family already there.

childSpans.title: Climbing the Hill
childSpans.description: The three girls, in their colored sunbonnets, climb the sliding, slipping hill toward the beach.

childSpans.title: Observing the Samuel Josephs
childSpans.description: The girls pause at the top of the hill and observe the Samuel Josephs family with their lady-help already at the beach.

childSpans.title: At the Beach
childSpans.description: The Burnell girls encounter the Trout boys and witness their discoveries in the sand.

childSpans.title: The Trout Boys' Boot Discovery
childSpans.description: Pip and Rags show the Burnell girls an old, wet, squashed-looking boot they found in the sand.

childSpans.title: Pip Explains Buried Treasure
childSpans.description: Pip explains that many things are buried in the sand from wrecks, and Rags pours water to moisten the sand for easier digging.

childSpans.title: The Emerald Revelation
childSpans.description: Pip mysteriously reveals a green emerald he found, making the girls promise secrecy and performing an elaborate ritual before showing them the jewel.

childSpans.title: The Beach Gathering
childSpans.description: Women and children arrive at the beach for their designated bathing time

childSpans.title: Arrival and Preparation
childSpans.description: The summer colony women and children arrive and prepare for bathing

childSpans.title: Parties Arrive Over Sand-Hills
childSpans.description: Whole parties appear over the sand-hills and come down to the beach

childSpans.title: Women and Children Undress
childSpans.description: Women undress and don bathing dresses and caps; children are unbuttoned

childSpans.title: Mrs. Fairfield Gathers Her Brood
childSpans.description: Old Mrs. Fairfield gathers the children and gets them ready, sitting with her knitting-bag

childSpans.title: Children Enter the Water
childSpans.description: The Trout boys and Burnell girls enter the water with varying degrees of bravery

childSpans.title: Trout Boys Enter Water
childSpans.description: Pip and Rags whip their shirts over their heads and enter the water without hesitation

childSpans.title: Burnell Girls Enter Water
childSpans.description: Isabel and Kezia follow on the understanding they will not be splashed

childSpans.title: Lottie at the Water's Edge
childSpans.description: Lottie sits at the edge of the water making vague motions with her arms, then flees from a large wave

childSpans.title: Beryl and Mrs. Kember
childSpans.description: Beryl entrusts her jewelry to Mrs. Fairfield and encounters Mrs. Harry Kember on the beach

childSpans.title: Beryl Deposits Her Jewelry
childSpans.description: Beryl gives her rings and chain to Mrs. Fairfield and announces she will bathe with Mrs. Harry Kember

childSpans.title: Beryl Gives Jewelry to Mrs. Fairfield
childSpans.description: Beryl drops two rings and a thin gold chain into Mrs. Fairfield's lap

childSpans.title: Beryl Announces Bathing with Mrs. Kember
childSpans.description: Beryl vaguely announces she will bathe with Mrs. Harry Kember, causing Mrs. Fairfield's disapproval

childSpans.title: Mrs. Harry Kember Introduced
childSpans.description: Beryl meets Mrs. Harry Kember on the stones and learns about her character and reputation

childSpans.title: Beryl Meets Mrs. Kember
childSpans.description: Beryl finds Mrs. Kember sitting hunched on the stones smoking, who comments on Beryl's pleased appearance

childSpans.title: Mrs. Kember's Character and Reputation
childSpans.description: Detailed description of Mrs. Kember's appearance, habits, and scandalous reputation at the Bay

childSpans.title: Description of Harry Kember
childSpans.description: Detailed description of Mrs. Kember's mysterious, handsome husband and the rumors surrounding him

childSpans.title: Undressing and Seduction
childSpans.description: Beryl and Mrs. Kember undress for bathing; Mrs. Kember seduces Beryl with flattery and boldness

childSpans.title: Mrs. Kember Undresses
childSpans.description: Mrs. Kember rises, yawns, and begins to undress, revealing her plain underclothes

childSpans.title: Beryl Undresses and Feels Seduced
childSpans.description: Beryl undresses while Mrs. Kember flatters her, calling her a little beauty and touching her waist

childSpans.title: Beryl Dons Bathing-Dress
childSpans.description: Beryl puts on her damp bathing-dress while Mrs. Kember encourages her to abandon shyness

childSpans.title: Bathing Together
childSpans.description: Beryl and Mrs. Kember enter the water together; Mrs. Kember offers worldly advice and reveals her unsettling resemblance to her husband

childSpans.title: Enter the Water Together
childSpans.description: Beryl and Mrs. Kember walk down the beach together and enter the warm, transparent blue water

childSpans.title: Beryl Stands in the Water
childSpans.description: Beryl stands with arms outstretched, jumping gently with each wave as Mrs. Kember offers worldly advice

childSpans.title: Mrs. Kember Swims and Returns
childSpans.description: Mrs. Kember turns turtle and swims away quickly, then returns, appearing like a caricature of her husband

childSpans.title: Linda's Garden Solitude
childSpans.description: Linda lies in the garden alone while the household is at the beach, observing flowers and reflecting on life's transience.

childSpans.title: Linda in the Steamer Chair
childSpans.description: Linda lies under the manuka tree, observing the flowers and the sleeping boy beside her, contemplating solitude and the garden.

childSpans.title: Observation of Manuka Flowers
childSpans.description: Linda observes the manuka flowers falling, contemplating their beauty and wastefulness.

childSpans.title: The Sleeping Boy
childSpans.description: Linda notices her infant son sleeping beside her on pillows.

childSpans.title: Garden Flowers and Life's Transience
childSpans.description: Linda observes the bright flowers in the garden and reflects on the fleeting nature of life and beauty.

childSpans.title: Observation of Garden Flowers
childSpans.description: Linda contemplates the picotees, marigolds, and nasturtiums, reflecting on the inability to truly know them before life sweeps one away.

childSpans.title: Linda's Memory and Marriage Reflection
childSpans.description: Linda recalls her childhood promise with her father to escape, her meeting with Stanley, and her complex feelings about her marriage and motherhood.

childSpans.title: Childhood Memory of Escape
childSpans.description: Linda recalls sitting on the veranda of their Tasmanian home with her father, who promised they would escape together.

childSpans.title: Father's Promise of Escape
childSpans.description: Linda's father promises to escape with her, mentioning sailing up a river in China.

childSpans.title: Stanley's Appearance
childSpans.description: A young man with bright ginger hair walks past, and Linda's father teases her about her 'beau,' introducing Stanley Burnell.

childSpans.title: Linda's Reflection on Stanley
childSpans.description: Linda reflects on her marriage to Stanley, distinguishing between the public Stanley and the private, sensitive man she loves.

childSpans.title: Stanley's True Nature
childSpans.description: Linda describes the timid, sensitive, innocent Stanley who prays and longs to be good, contrasting him with the public Stanley.

childSpans.title: The Burden of Marriage
childSpans.description: Linda reflects on how rarely she sees her true Stanley, and how her life is spent rescuing and calming him, with dread of childbearing.

childSpans.title: Linda's Crisis About Motherhood
childSpans.description: Linda confronts her deepest conflict: her lack of love for her children and the damage childbearing has done to her.

childSpans.title: Revelation of Maternal Indifference
childSpans.description: Linda admits to herself that she does not love her children, that childbearing has broken her, and that she has no warmth left to give them.

childSpans.title: The Boy's Awakening and Connection
childSpans.description: The infant boy wakes and smiles at his mother, leading to a moment of unexpected emotional connection between them.

childSpans.title: The Boy Wakes and Smiles
childSpans.description: The boy turns over, opens his eyes, and smiles at his mother with a toothless beam.

childSpans.title: Boy's Awakening
childSpans.description: The boy turns over and opens his dark-blue eyes, looking at his mother.

childSpans.title: Boy's Smile
childSpans.description: The boy's face dimples and breaks into a wide, toothless smile, seeming to ask why his mother doesn't like him.

childSpans.title: Linda's Rejection and Unexpected Connection
childSpans.description: Linda initially rejects the boy coldly, but then experiences a profound emotional shift and connection with him.

childSpans.title: Linda's Cold Rejection
childSpans.description: Linda tells the boy coldly that she doesn't like babies, and questions why he keeps smiling.

childSpans.title: Emotional Breakthrough
childSpans.description: Linda is astonished by the boy's confidence and experiences a sudden emotional shift, whispering 'Hallo, my funny!' with tears in her eyes.

childSpans.title: Boy's Play with Pink Object
childSpans.description: The boy becomes distracted by something pink and soft waving in front of him, attempting to catch it and rolling over in the effort.

childSpans.title: The Deserted Beach at Midday
childSpans.description: Vivid description of the beach at low tide, the summer colony in siesta, and the natural landscape under intense sun.

childSpans.title: The Beach Landscape
childSpans.description: Description of the deserted beach with tide out, sand, pebbles, and the effects of intense sun.

childSpans.title: Tide Out
childSpans.description: The beach is deserted with the tide out and warm sea lapping lazily.

childSpans.title: Sun's Effects on the Beach
childSpans.description: The sun beats down hot and fiery, baking pebbles, sucking up water, and bleaching convolvulus flowers.

childSpans.title: The Rock Pools
childSpans.description: Detailed observation of the weed-hung rocks and the miniature worlds within the rock pools.

childSpans.title: Miniature Worlds in Rock Pools
childSpans.description: Each rock pool appears as a lake with houses, mountains, and underwater life; mysterious sounds and movements occur within.

childSpans.title: Summer Colony in Siesta
childSpans.description: The summer colony bungalows with green blinds drawn, bathing dresses and towels scattered, and the landscape in heat haze.

childSpans.title: Colony at Rest
childSpans.description: The bungalows are shuttered with green blinds, bathing clothes scattered about, and the bush quivering in heat haze.

childSpans.title: Snooker's Heat Exhaustion
childSpans.description: The Trouts' dog Snooker lies stretched in the middle of the sandy road, apparently giving up from the heat.

childSpans.title: Kezia and Grandmother's Siesta
childSpans.description: Kezia and her grandmother share a siesta in their bedroom, where Kezia observes her grandmother staring at the wall and initiates a conversation about mortality.

childSpans.title: The Bedroom Setting
childSpans.description: Description of the shared bedroom where Kezia and her grandmother rest, with details of the simple furnishings and objects.

childSpans.title: Bedroom Description
childSpans.description: The bedroom is simply furnished with light varnished wood, bare floor, and makeshift furniture including a packing-case dressing-table.

childSpans.title: Kezia's Observation
childSpans.description: Kezia asks her grandmother why she keeps staring at the wall, initiating their conversation.

childSpans.title: The Story of Uncle William
childSpans.description: Grandmother reveals she was thinking of Kezia's Uncle William who died of sunstroke in the mines, and Kezia learns about his death.

childSpans.title: Uncle William's Death Revealed
childSpans.description: Grandmother tells Kezia about Uncle William who went to the mines, got sunstroke, and died.

childSpans.title: Kezia's Questions About Death
childSpans.description: Kezia asks if it makes grandmother sad, and then questions why Uncle William had to die and whether everybody must die.

childSpans.title: Dialogue on Mortality and Acceptance
childSpans.description: Grandmother and Kezia discuss the inevitability of death, with Kezia expressing fear and resistance, and grandmother accepting it as natural.

childSpans.title: Kezia's Defiance of Death
childSpans.description: Kezia asks if she must die and suggests she simply won't, expressing childish defiance against mortality.

childSpans.title: Kezia Demands a Promise
childSpans.description: Kezia becomes distressed at the thought of her grandmother dying and demands a promise that grandmother will never die and leave her.

childSpans.title: Physical Affection and Play
childSpans.description: Kezia leaps onto her grandmother's lap and covers her with kisses and tickles, and grandmother reciprocates, both laughing together.

childSpans.title: Kezia's Kisses and Tickles
childSpans.description: Kezia leaps onto grandmother's knees, clasps her throat, and covers her with kisses while pleading 'say never' and tickling her.

childSpans.title: Grandmother's Reciprocation
childSpans.description: Grandmother drops her knitting, swings back in the rocker, and begins tickling Kezia in return, both laughing together.

childSpans.title: The Forgotten Promise
childSpans.description: Grandmother calls an end to the play, and both have forgotten what the 'never' promise was about.

childSpans.title: Alice's Departure and Journey
childSpans.description: Alice leaves the Burnell household and walks toward Mrs. Stubbs' shop

childSpans.title: Alice Leaves the Burnell House
childSpans.description: Alice exits the back door dressed for her afternoon out

childSpans.title: Alice's Exit
childSpans.description: Alice walks down the path to the gate in her conspicuous outfit

childSpans.title: Beryl's Judgment
childSpans.description: Beryl observes Alice from the window and judges her appearance

childSpans.title: Alice's Walk to the Shop
childSpans.description: Alice walks along the road toward Mrs. Stubbs' shop, feeling anxious about being alone

childSpans.title: Alice's Anxiety on the Road
childSpans.description: Alice feels uneasy walking alone and speaks to the distant gum-tree

childSpans.title: Mrs. Stubbs' Shop Described
childSpans.description: The narrator describes the appearance and contents of Mrs. Stubbs' shop

childSpans.title: Alice at Mrs. Stubbs' Shop
childSpans.description: Alice arrives at the shop and has tea with Mrs. Stubbs, who shows her photographs

childSpans.title: Alice Arrives at the Shop
childSpans.description: Alice enters Mrs. Stubbs' shop and is warmly welcomed

childSpans.title: Alice Enters the Shop
childSpans.description: Alice presses open the door and is greeted by Mrs. Stubbs

childSpans.title: Tea is Laid Out
childSpans.description: Mrs. Stubbs prepares tea on the parlour table while the Primus stove roars

childSpans.title: Mrs. Stubbs Shows Photographs
childSpans.description: Mrs. Stubbs reveals and discusses her new photographs with Alice

childSpans.title: Photographs Revealed
childSpans.description: Mrs. Stubbs discloses a large brown-paper parcel containing new photographs

childSpans.title: Alice Examines the Photographs
childSpans.description: Alice examines the photographs and Mrs. Stubbs discusses her preference for size

childSpans.title: Discussion of Mrs. Stubbs' Late Husband
childSpans.description: Mrs. Stubbs discusses her late husband's death from dropsy and shows his portrait

childSpans.title: Freedom and Reflection
childSpans.description: Mrs. Stubbs declares that freedom is best, and Alice reflects on her own situation

childSpans.title: Mrs. Stubbs Declares Freedom is Best
childSpans.description: Mrs. Stubbs unexpectedly proclaims that freedom is best

childSpans.title: Alice's Awkward Reaction
childSpans.description: Alice reacts awkwardly to the declaration of freedom and reflects on her own kitchen

childSpans.title: Assembly and Game Setup
childSpans.description: The children gather in the washhouse and establish the rules of their animal-themed card game.

childSpans.title: The Washhouse Setting
childSpans.description: Description of the washhouse as an ideal location for the children's gathering, with details of its contents and atmosphere.

childSpans.title: Choosing Animal Roles
childSpans.description: The children debate and select their animal roles for the game, with Kezia insisting on being a bee despite objections.

childSpans.title: Explaining the Card Game
childSpans.description: Pip, as the bull, explains the rules of the matching card game to the other children, particularly to Lottie who struggles to understand.

childSpans.title: The Game in Progress
childSpans.description: The children play the card game with increasing excitement and engagement, making animal sounds and competing.

childSpans.title: Cards Are Dealt and Game Begins
childSpans.description: Pip deals the cards and the game commences with the children making their animal sounds and playing their cards.

childSpans.title: Lottie Forgets Her Role
childSpans.description: Lottie becomes confused about her animal role and the other children encourage her to change to a dog instead.

childSpans.title: The Mysterious Knocking
childSpans.description: Pip stops the game when he hears a strange knocking sound, causing the children to become alert and frightened.

childSpans.title: Encroaching Darkness and Growing Fear
childSpans.description: As evening falls and darkness descends, the children become increasingly frightened in the washhouse, imagining dangers and feeling abandoned.

childSpans.title: The Day Fades to Darkness
childSpans.description: The sunset fades and darkness rapidly approaches, transforming the washhouse atmosphere from playful to ominous.

childSpans.title: The Spider Story
childSpans.description: Pip tells a frightening story about a giant spider, causing the children to huddle together in fear.

childSpans.title: Fear of Abandonment
childSpans.description: The children worry that the adults have forgotten them and deliberately left them alone in the darkening washhouse.

childSpans.title: The Face at the Window and Resolution
childSpans.description: A mysterious face appears at the window, terrifying the children, but it is revealed to be Uncle Jonathan arriving to collect the Trout boys.

childSpans.title: Lottie's Piercing Scream
childSpans.description: Lottie screams at the sight of a pale face with black eyes and beard pressed against the window, causing all the children to panic.

childSpans.title: Uncle Jonathan's Arrival
childSpans.description: The door opens and Uncle Jonathan is revealed, having come to collect the Trout boys, resolving the children's terror.

childSpans.title: Jonathan's Visit to the Burnells
childSpans.description: Jonathan arrives at the Burnell household and spends time with Linda in the garden, discussing his life and work

childSpans.title: Garden Encounter
childSpans.description: Jonathan finds Linda in the front garden and they settle in the garden to talk

childSpans.title: Jonathan's Arrival
childSpans.description: Jonathan encounters Linda in the front garden tending to flowers

e001.description: White sea-mist covers the whole of Crescent Bay, hiding the landscape including hills, paddocks, bungalows, sandy road, white dunes, beach, and sea.

e002.description: Heavy dew has fallen on the landscape, covering grass with blue color, hanging on bushes, and bowing flowers and plants to the earth with wetness.

e003.description: Sounds emerge from the bush: little streams flowing quickly and lightly between smooth stones, gushing into ferny basins, splashing of big drops on large leaves, and a faint stirring and shaking with the snapping of a twig, followed by silence as if someone is listening.

e004.description: A flock of sheep comes pattering around the corner of Crescent Bay between piled-up masses of broken rock, huddled together as a small, tossing, woolly mass with thin, stick-like legs trotting quickly as if frightened by cold and quiet.

e005.description: The shepherd appears in the rocky gateway, described as a lean, upright old man wearing a frieze coat covered with dew drops, velvet trousers tied under the knee, and a wide-awake hat with a folded blue handkerchief around the brim. He carries a smooth yellow stick and keeps up soft, light whistling that sounds mournful and tender.

e006.description: The sheep begin to bleat, and ghostly flocks and herds answer them from under the sea, creating a call-and-response pattern of 'Baa! Baaa!'

e007.description: The shepherd and flock pass by the big gum-tree outside Mrs. Stubbs' shop, an enormous shock-haired giant with arms stretched out, releasing a strong whiff of eucalyptus.

e008.description: The mist dissolves rapidly as the sun rises, thinning and speeding away from the shallow plain, rolling up from the bush and disappearing as if in a hurry to escape. Big twists and curls jostle and shoulder each other as silvery beams broaden. The far-away sky becomes bright and pure blue, reflected in puddles, and drops on telegraph poles flash into points of light.

e009.description: The shepherd draws a small pipe from his breast pocket, fumbles for a chunk of speckled tobacco, pares off a few shavings, and stuffs the bowl. He lights up and blue smoke wreathed his head.

e010.description: The dog, watching the shepherd light his pipe, looks proud of him.

e011.description: The sheep's bleating reaches the ears of sleeping inhabitants and children in the summer colony, sounding in their dreams as they lift their arms to drag down and cuddle darling little woolly lambs of sleep.

e012.description: The Burnells' cat Florrie appears, sitting on the gatepost far too early as usual, looking for their milk-girl.

e013.description: When Florrie sees the old sheep-dog, she sprang up quickly, arched her back, drew in her tabby head, and gave a little fastidious shiver, saying 'Ugh! What a coarse, revolting creature!' The old sheep-dog, not looking up, waggled past, flinging out his legs from side to side, with only one ear twitching to prove he saw her and thought her a silly young female.

e014.description: The breeze of morning lifts in the bush, and the smell of leaves and wet black earth mingles with the sharp smell of the sea. Myriads of birds are singing.

e015.description: A goldfinch flies over the shepherd's head and, perching on the tiptop of a spray, turns to the sun, ruffling its small breast feathers.

e016.description: The shepherd and flock pass the fisherman's hut and the charred-looking little whare where Leila the milk-girl lived with her old Gran.

e017.description: The shepherd and flock pass by the charred-looking whare where Leila and her Gran live.

e018.description: The sheep stray over a yellow swamp and Wag, the sheep-dog, paddles after them, rounds them up, and heads them for the steeper, narrower rocky pass that led out of Crescent Bay and towards Daylight Cove.

e019.description: Wag runs out along a ledge of rock after something that smelled, and runs back again disgusted.

e020.description: The shepherd puts away his pipe, dropping it into his breast-pocket so that the little bowl hangs over, and straightway the soft airy whistling begins again.

e021.description: The sheep, pushing, nudging, and hurrying, round the bend and the shepherd follows after out of sight.

e022.description: Stanley Burnell exits the back door of a bungalow in a broad-striped bathing suit

e023.description: Stanley races across the paddock, clears the stile, rushes through tussock grass, staggers up the sandy hillock, and races over stones and pebbles onto the hard sand, reaching the sea with splashing sounds

e024.description: Stanley wades out into the water exulting, believing himself to be first man in as usual, having beaten everyone else

e025.description: Stanley swoops down to souse his head and neck in the water

e026.description: A velvety bass voice booms across the water, hailing Stanley with 'Hail, brother! All hail, Thou Mighty One!'

e027.description: Stanley lifts up to see a dark head bobbing far out in the water with an arm lifted, discovering it is Jonathan Trout already in the sea before him

e028.description: Jonathan sings out 'Glorious morning!' from the water

e029.description: Stanley responds briefly to Jonathan's greeting with 'Yes, very fine!'

e030.description: Stanley internally questions why Jonathan is in his spot and begins swimming overarm to compete with him

e031.description: Jonathan shouts 'I had an extraordinary dream last night!' while swimming

e032.description: Stanley turns over on his back and kicks with his legs violently until he becomes a living waterspout, attempting to avoid Jonathan's conversation

e033.description: Jonathan describes his dream: 'I dreamed I was hanging over a terrifically high cliff, shouting to some one below.'

e034.description: Stanley stops his violent splashing and addresses Jonathan directly

e035.description: Stanley tells Jonathan 'Look here, Trout, I'm in rather a hurry this morning.'

e036.description: Jonathan is surprised or pretends to be surprised, sinking under the water then reappearing and blowing

e037.description: Stanley explains to Jonathan: 'All I mean is, I've no time to—to—to fool about. I want to get this over. I'm in a hurry. I've work to do this morning—see?'

e038.description: Jonathan departs, saying 'Pass, friend!' and sliding away through the water with scarcely a ripple

e039.description: Stanley internally curses Jonathan, thinking 'But curse the fellow! He'd ruined Stanley's bathe. What an unpractical idiot the man was!'

e040.description: Stanley strikes out to sea again, then quickly swims back in again

e041.description: Stanley rushes away up the beach, feeling cheated

e042.description: Jonathan stays in the water longer, floating gently and moving his hands like fins, letting the sea rock his long, skinny body

e043.description: Jonathan reflects that despite his fiendish desire to tease Stanley sometimes, he is fond of him at bottom and feels sorry for him. He recognizes something pathetic in Stanley's determination to make a job of everything and worries he will be caught out one day.

e044.description: An immense wave lifts Jonathan, rides past him, and breaks along the beach with a joyful sound. Another wave follows.

e045.description: Jonathan articulates his life philosophy: to live carelessly and recklessly, spending oneself; to take things easy and not fight against the ebb and flow of life, but to give way to it. He reflects that tension is all wrong and that the perfect morning seems to whisper 'Why not?'

e046.description: Jonathan turns blue with cold as he exits the water. He aches all over as though someone is wringing the blood out of him.

e047.description: Jonathan stalks up the beach shivering, with all his muscles tight

e048.description: Jonathan realizes his bathe is spoilt because he stayed in the water too long

e049.description: Stanley Burnell enters the living-room wearing a blue serge suit, stiff collar, and spotted tie. He looks almost uncannily clean and brushed, indicating he is preparing to go to town for the day. He drops into his chair, pulls out his watch, and places it beside his plate.

e050.description: Stanley announces that he has only twenty-five minutes and asks Beryl to check if the porridge is ready.

e051.description: Beryl sits down at the table and pours out Stanley's tea. Stanley takes a sip and discovers that Beryl has forgotten to add sugar.

e052.description: Stanley's blue eyes widen and quiver as he notices the forgotten sugar. He shoots a quick glance at Beryl and leans back, sensing something is wrong.

e053.description: Stanley asks Beryl if something is wrong, noting that she seems rather strange. Beryl deflects, saying nothing is wrong and asking why there should be. Stanley begins to question her further but is interrupted.

e054.description: The three little girls enter the living-room, each carrying a porridge plate. They are dressed alike in blue jerseys and knickers with bare brown legs and hair plaited and pinned up in a horse's tail. Behind them comes Mrs. Fairfield with the tray.

e055.description: Mrs. Fairfield warns the children to be careful and asks if they have said good morning to their father. The children respond affirmatively and settle themselves on the bench opposite Stanley and Beryl. Mrs. Fairfield greets Stanley and gives him his plate.

e056.description: Stanley asks Mrs. Fairfield how the boy is. She responds that he only woke up once last night and remarks on what a perfect morning it is. She pauses with her hand on the loaf of bread to gaze out of the open door into the garden, where the sea can be heard. The sun streams through the wide-open window, illuminating the yellow varnished walls and bare floor. Everything on the table flashes and glitters. In the middle is an old salad bowl filled with yellow and red nasturtiums. Mrs. Fairfield smiles with deep contentment.

e057.description: Beryl scolds Kezia for being a messy child, asking why she cannot eat her food properly like Isabel and Lottie. Kezia stares at Beryl in confusion, having only dug a river down the middle of her porridge and filled it, eating the banks away—something she does every morning without complaint.

e058.description: Kezia defends herself by pointing out that Lottie always makes a floating island with her porridge. Lottie denies this, and Isabel interjects smartly, saying she just sprinkles her porridge with sugar, puts on milk, and finishes it, claiming that only babies play with their food.

e059.description: Stanley pushes back his chair and stands up, preparing to leave the table.

e060.description: Stanley asks Mrs. Fairfield to get him his shoes and instructs Beryl to go to the gate and stop the coach. He asks Isabel to run to her mother and ask where his bowler hat has been put. He then asks if the children have been playing with his stick.

e061.description: Stanley begins to bluster about his missing stick, claiming he distinctly remembers putting it in the corner. He demands that it be found immediately, saying there is no time to lose.

e062.description: Alice, the servant girl, is drawn into the search for the stick. She asks Stanley if he has been using it to poke the kitchen fire with by any chance.

e063.description: Stanley dashes into the bedroom where Linda is lying. He tells her about the missing stick, expressing his frustration that he cannot keep a single possession to himself.

e064.description: Linda responds vaguely to Stanley's complaint about the stick, asking what stick. Stanley decides that her vagueness cannot be real and wonders if anyone will sympathize with him.

e065.description: Beryl's voice cries from the gate that the coach is waiting for Stanley.

e066.description: Stanley waves his arm to Linda, saying there is no time to say good-bye, intending this as a punishment to her. He snatches his bowler hat and dashes out of the house.

e067.description: Stanley swings down the garden path toward the gate where the coach is waiting. Beryl is leaning over the open gate, laughing up at somebody, seemingly unconcerned about Stanley's departure. Stanley observes this and thinks about the heartlessness of women.

e068.description: Kelly trails his whip across the horses. Stanley shouts good-bye to Beryl for the sake of appearances. Beryl turns, gives a little skip, and runs back to the house. Stanley observes that she seems glad to be rid of him.

e069.description: Beryl runs into the living-room and calls out 'He's gone!' announcing Stanley's departure to the household.

e070.description: Linda cries from her room asking if Stanley has gone. Old Mrs. Fairfield appears, carrying the boy in his little flannel coatee, and asks 'Gone?' The household confirms 'Gone!'

e071.description: The household experiences a dramatic shift in atmosphere. The relief of having the man out of the house is palpable. Their voices change as they call to one another, sounding warm, loving, and as if they share a secret.

e072.description: Beryl goes over to the table and offers Mrs. Fairfield another cup of tea, saying it is still hot. She expresses her desire to celebrate the fact that they can do what they like now, with no man to disturb them and the whole perfect day theirs.

e073.description: Mrs. Fairfield declines the tea but demonstrates her agreement with Beryl's sentiment by tossing the boy up and saying 'a-goos-a-goos-a-ga!' to him, indicating she feels the same relief and joy.

e074.description: The little girls run into the paddock like chickens let out of a coop, expressing their freedom and joy at Stanley's departure.

e075.description: Alice, the servant girl, washing up the dishes in the kitchen, catches the infection of joy and uses the precious tank water in a perfectly reckless fashion. She expresses disdain for men, plunging the teapot into the bowl and holding it under the water even after it has stopped bubbling, as if drowning a man.

e076.description: Lottie struggles to cross the stile, her knees wobbling as she grasps the post, unable to decide which leg to put over first.

e077.description: Isabel urges Kezia not to wait for Lottie, calling her a silly girl who makes a fuss, and offers Kezia her larger bucket as an incentive to come with her.

e078.description: Kezia refuses to leave Lottie alone and runs back to help her cross the stile by instructing her on foot placement.

e079.description: Lottie successfully crosses the stile by turning around, sitting down, and sliding over. She expresses hope that she is improving at climbing over stiles.

e080.description: The three girls, in their colored sunbonnets, climb the sliding, slipping hill toward the beach, pausing at the top to observe who is already there.

e081.description: The girls observe the Samuel Josephs family already at the beach with their lady-help, who maintains strict order through a whistle and cane, organizing competitions and races with prizes from a string kit. The narrative reflects on the Burnell children's past experience with the Samuel Josephs and their mediocre parties.

e082.description: The Trout boys, Pip and Rags, are discovered by the Burnell girls digging in the sand near the water. Pip shows them an old, wet, squashed-looking boot he has found.

e083.description: Kezia questions what Pip intends to do with the boot, and Pip scornfully responds that he will keep it because it is a find.

e084.description: Pip explains that many things are buried in the sand from shipwrecks, including potential treasure, and asks why Rags continues to pour water.

e085.description: Rags pours water from a small bucket into the sand to moisten it, making the digging work easier. The water turns brown like cocoa as it mixes with the sand.

e086.description: Pip mysteriously announces he will show the girls something he found yesterday, makes them promise secrecy by saying 'cross my heart straight dinkum,' and sticks his spade into the sand in preparation.

e087.description: Pip performs an elaborate ritual to reveal his treasure: he takes something from his pocket, rubs it on his jersey, breathes on it, rubs it again, makes the girls turn around and look the same way, and then opens his hand to reveal a flashing, winking green object.

e088.description: Pip reveals the green object to be an emerald, which is as big as a star and far more beautiful than the small emerald in Aunt Beryl's ring. Even Isabel is impressed by the discovery.

e089.description: Whole parties appear over the sand-hills and come down on the beach to bathe as the morning lengthens. It is understood that at eleven o'clock the women and children of the summer colony have the sea to themselves.

e090.description: The women undress and pull on their bathing dresses, covering their heads in hideous caps like sponge bags. The children are unbuttoned. The beach becomes strewn with little heaps of clothes and shoes, with big summer hats held down by stones.

e091.description: Old Mrs. Fairfield, in a lilac cotton dress and black hat, gathers her little brood and gets them ready. The little Trout boys whip their shirts over their heads, and the five children speed toward the water while their grandma sits with her knitting-bag ready.

e092.description: Pip and Rags, shivering and crouching down, slap the water and never hesitate as they enter the sea. They are tender, delicate-looking little boys who are braver than the firm compact little girls.

e093.description: Isabel, who can swim twelve strokes, and Kezia, who can nearly swim eight, follow into the water on the strict understanding they are not to be splashed.

e094.description: Lottie sits at the edge of the water with her legs straight and knees pressed together, making vague motions with her arms. When a large wave comes, she scrambles to her feet with horror and flies up the beach again.

e095.description: Beryl drops two rings and a thin gold chain into Mrs. Fairfield's lap, asking her to keep them while she bathes.

e096.description: Mrs. Fairfield asks if Beryl is going to bathe there. Beryl drawls vaguely that she is undressing farther along and will bathe with Mrs. Harry Kember.

e097.description: Mrs. Fairfield's lips set in disapproval at Beryl's announcement that she will bathe with Mrs. Harry Kember. Beryl knows of her mother's disapproval.

e098.description: Beryl skims over the stones toward Mrs. Harry Kember, who sits hunched up on the stones with her arms round her knees, smoking. Beryl smiles down at her, expressing joy at being young.

e099.description: Detailed description of Mrs. Harry Kember's appearance and character: a long, strange-looking woman with narrow hands and feet, exhausted face, burnt-out fair curled fringe. She is the only woman at the Bay who smokes incessantly. She is described as parched, withered, and cold, lying in the sun like driftwood. The women at the Bay think she is very fast, lacking vanity, using slang, treating men as equals, and not caring about her house. She calls her servant Gladys 'Glad-eyes,' which is considered scandalous.

e100.description: Description of Mrs. Kember's husband, Harry Kember: at least ten years younger than she is, incredibly handsome like a mask or American novel illustration. He has black hair, dark blue eyes, red lips, slow sleepy smile. He is a fine tennis player and perfect dancer. He is mysterious, seemingly walking in his sleep. Men cannot get a word out of him; he ignores his wife as she ignores him. There are rumors about him, including speculation that he might commit murder. Women imagine him with Mrs. Kember's body stretched on the beach, cold, bloody, and still with a cigarette in her mouth.

e101.description: Mrs. Kember rises, yawns, unsnaps her belt buckle, and tugs at the tape of her blouse. She begins to undress, revealing her blue cotton knickers and linen bodice that reminds one of a pillow-case.

e102.description: Beryl steps out of her skirt and sheds her jersey, standing up in her short white petticoat and camisole with ribbon bows on the shoulders. Mrs. Kember exclaims 'Mercy on us, what a little beauty you are!' Beryl says 'Don't!' softly but feels a little beauty as she draws off her stockings.

e103.description: Mrs. Kember asks why Beryl doesn't wear stays and touches Beryl's waist. Beryl springs away with a small affected cry and says 'Never!' firmly. Mrs. Kember sighs 'Lucky little creature' while unfastening her own stays. Beryl turns her back and begins the complicated movements of trying to take off her clothes and pull on her bathing-dress at the same time.

e104.description: Mrs. Kember tells Beryl not to mind her and asks why be shy, saying she won't eat her or be shocked like the other ninnies. She gives a strange neighing laugh and grimaces at the other women. Beryl is shy and never undresses in front of anybody. Mrs. Kember makes her feel it is silly and something to be ashamed of. Beryl glances at her friend standing boldly in her torn chemise and lighting a fresh cigarette. A quick, bold, evil feeling starts up in Beryl's breast. Laughing recklessly, she draws on the limp, sandy-feeling bathing-dress and fastens the twisted buttons.

e105.description: Beryl and Mrs. Kember begin to go down the beach together toward the water. The water is quite warm, marvellous transparent blue flecked with silver, with gold-colored sand at the bottom. When Beryl kicks with her toes, a little puff of gold-dust rises.

e106.description: Beryl stands in the water with her arms outstretched, gazing out. As each wave comes, she gives the slightest little jump, so that it seems the wave lifts her gently. Mrs. Kember says 'I believe in pretty girls having a good time. Why not? Don't you make a mistake, my dear. Enjoy yourself.' She suddenly turns turtle, disappears, and swims away quickly like a rat.

e107.description: Mrs. Kember flicks round and begins swimming back. Beryl feels she is being poisoned by this cold woman but longs to hear what she will say. As Mrs. Kember comes up close, she looks in her black waterproof bathing-cap, with her sleepy face lifted above the water, just her chin touching, like a horrible caricature of her husband.

e108.description: Linda lies in a steamer chair under a manuka tree in the garden, observing the tiny yellowish flowers falling and contemplating their beauty and transience.

e109.description: Linda observes her infant son sleeping beside her on pillows, noting his fine dark hair and bright coral ear. She feels pleasant knowing the bungalows are empty and she is alone.

e110.description: Linda observes the bright flowers in the garden—picotees, marigolds, and nasturtiums—and reflects on the inability to truly know them before life sweeps one away.

e111.description: Linda recalls sitting on the veranda of her Tasmanian home, leaning against her father's knee. Her father promises that when they are old enough, they will escape together, mentioning his fancy to sail up a river in China.

e112.description: A young man with bright ginger hair walks slowly past Linda's house. Her father teases her, calling him 'Linny's beau,' and Linda responds with the thought 'Oh, papa, fancy being married to Stanley Burnell!'

e113.description: Linda reflects on her marriage to Stanley, distinguishing between the public Stanley and the private, sensitive, innocent Stanley who prays and longs to be good. She notes that Stanley is simple and cannot be disloyal or tell a lie.

e114.description: Linda reflects on how rarely she sees her true Stanley. She describes her life as spent rescuing, restoring, and calming him, and her time is consumed by dread of having children. She feels like she is living in a house that catches on fire or a ship that gets wrecked every day.

e115.description: Linda confronts her deepest conflict: she does not love her children. She admits that childbearing has broken her, made her weak, and left her with no warmth to give her children. She is indifferent about her infant son, who has been cared for by her mother and Beryl.

e116.description: The boy turns over in his sleep and opens his dark-blue baby eyes, looking at his mother as if peeping at her.

e117.description: The boy's face dimples and breaks into a wide, toothless smile, a perfect beam. His smile seems to say 'I'm here! Why don't you like me?'

e118.description: Linda smiles at the boy's smile but then checks herself and says to him coldly, 'I don't like babies.' The boy cannot believe her and asks 'Don't like me?' while waving his arms foolishly. Linda drops off her chair onto the grass and asks severely why he keeps smiling, saying if he knew what she was thinking he wouldn't smile.

e119.description: Linda is astonished by the boy's confidence and his knowing smile. She experiences a sudden emotional shift, realizing her true feeling is not indifference but something new and profound. Tears dance in her eyes as she breathes in a small whisper to the boy, 'Hallo, my funny!'

e120.description: The boy becomes serious and distracted by something pink and soft waving in front of him. He makes a grab at it and it disappears. When another appears, he determines to catch it, makes a tremendous effort, and rolls right over.

e121.description: The tide is out at Crescent Bay beach, leaving the beach deserted. The warm sea laps lazily.

e122.description: The sun beats down hot and fiery on the fine sand, baking pebbles, sucking up water from shells, and bleaching pink convolvulus flowers. Sand-hoppers are the only things moving on the beach.

e123.description: The weed-hung rocks at low tide contain small rock pools that function as miniature worlds. Sunlight spins in the pools like silver coins, creating dancing reflections. Each pool appears as a lake with pink and blue houses, mountains, ravines, and passes. Underwater, a sea-forest of pink thread-like trees, velvet anemones, and orange weeds waves. Mysterious movements and sounds occur within the pools.

e124.description: The summer colony bungalows have green blinds drawn during siesta. Exhausted-looking bathing-dresses and rough striped towels are scattered over verandas, paddocks, and fences. Sand-shoes and collections of pawa shells sit on back window sills. The bush quivers in a heat haze.

e125.description: The Trouts' dog Snooker lies stretched in the middle of the sandy road, apparently exhausted from the heat. His blue eye is turned up, his legs stuck out stiffly, and he gives occasional desperate-sounding puffs, as if he has decided to make an end of it and is waiting for a cart to come along.

e126.description: Kezia asks her grandmother why she keeps stopping and staring at the wall. Kezia and her grandmother are taking their siesta together in a simple bedroom. Kezia lies on puffed-up pillows wearing only her short drawers and under-bodice, while her grandmother sits in a rocker at the window wearing a white ruffled dressing-gown, with pink knitting in her lap.

e127.description: Mrs. Fairfield reveals that she was thinking of Kezia's Uncle William, her Australian uncle whom Kezia has never seen. She tells Kezia that Uncle William went to the mines, got a sunstroke there, and died. Kezia visualizes him as a little man fallen over like a tin soldier by the side of a big black hole.

e128.description: Kezia asks her grandmother if it makes her sad to think about Uncle William. She then asks why Uncle William had to die when he wasn't old. She asks if everybody has to die, and when her grandmother confirms it, Kezia asks incredulously if she herself must die. She suggests she simply won't die. Her grandmother explains that 'we're not asked' and that it happens to all of us sooner or later.

e129.description: Kezia lies still thinking about death and mortality. She realizes that dying means she would have to leave everywhere forever, including leaving her grandmother. She becomes distressed and rolls over quickly, calling out to her grandmother in a startled voice.

e130.description: Kezia demands that her grandmother promise never to die, saying she couldn't leave her and couldn't not be there. She pleads with her grandmother to promise she won't ever die. Her grandmother continues knitting silently. Kezia becomes increasingly desperate, demanding her grandmother 'say never.' When her grandmother remains silent, Kezia can't bear it any longer.

e131.description: Kezia rolls off her bed and leaps lightly onto her grandmother's knees. She clasps her hands around the old woman's throat and begins kissing her under the chin, behind the ear, and blowing down her neck. She gasps 'Say never... say never... say never' between the kisses. She then begins to tickle her grandmother very softly and lightly.

e132.description: Mrs. Fairfield drops her knitting and swings back in the rocker. She begins to tickle Kezia in return. Both of them lie laughing in each other's arms, with Kezia gurgling 'Say never, say never, say never' while they laugh. Mrs. Fairfield calls an end to the play, calling Kezia 'my squirrel' and 'my wild pony,' and straightens her cap.

e133.description: After the tickling play ends, both Kezia and her grandmother have forgotten what the 'never' promise was about. Mrs. Fairfield asks Kezia to pick up her knitting.

e134.description: Alice, the servant-girl, exits the back door of the Burnell house and walks down the path to the gate, dressed in a conspicuous white cotton dress with large red spots, white shoes, a leghorn hat with poppies, white gloves stained with iron-mould, and carrying a dashed-looking sunshade

e135.description: Beryl, sitting in the window and fanning her freshly-washed hair with a heart-shaped Fijian fan, observes Alice and judges her appearance as gaudy and conspicuous, though she later corrects her unfair assessment when she learns Alice is visiting Mrs. Stubbs for tea

e136.description: Alice walks along the sandy road toward Mrs. Stubbs' shop, feeling anxious about being alone and speaking to the distant gum-tree to reassure herself

e137.description: The narrator describes Mrs. Stubbs' shop, perched on a little hillock with two big windows arranged as precarious pyramids, a broad veranda displaying bathing-dresses and sandshoes, and a long-standing notice about a lost gold brooch

e138.description: Alice presses open the shop door, the bell jangles, the red serge curtains part, and Mrs. Stubbs appears with a broad smile and a long bacon knife in her hand, welcoming Alice warmly

e139.description: Tea is laid on the parlour table with ham, sardines, butter, and a large johnny cake. The Primus stove roars loudly, making conversation difficult. Alice sits on the edge of a basket-chair while Mrs. Stubbs pumps the stove higher

e140.description: Mrs. Stubbs whips the cushion off a chair and discloses a large brown-paper parcel containing her new photographs. She shows Alice at least three dozen photographs of herself posed in an arm-chair with studio backdrops including a waterfall, Grecian pillar, and snowy mountain

e141.description: Mrs. Stubbs discusses her preference for size in photographs, saying she is having an enlargement made and that she finds small photographs dis'eartening. She explains that her late husband also preferred size and couldn't stand anything small

e142.description: Mrs. Stubbs tells Alice about her late husband's death from dropsy, explaining that liquid was drawn from him at the hospital. She points dramatically to a life-size portrait of her burly husband with a dead white rose in his buttonhole, with the inscription 'Be not afraid, it is I.' below it

e143.description: Mrs. Stubbs unexpectedly declares that freedom is best, repeating the phrase twice. Her soft, fat chuckle sounds like a purr as she arches her plump neck, with the pale-blue bow on her frizzy hair quivering

e144.description: Alice reacts to Mrs. Stubbs' declaration of freedom with a loud, silly little titter, feeling awkward and confused by the statement

e145.description: Alice's mind flies back to her own kitchen, and she realizes she wants to be back in it again, despite her earlier desire for freedom and adventure

e146.description: A strange company of children assembles in the Burnells' washhouse after tea. They gather around a table to play a game, having chosen the washhouse because they can make as much noise as they like without interruption.

e147.description: Kezia insists on being a bee despite objections that a bee is not an animal but an insect. She argues stoutly that an insect must be an animal because it makes a noise, unlike a fish.

e148.description: Pip declares himself a bull and makes a tremendous bellowing sound that alarms Lottie.

e149.description: Rags chooses to be a sheep, explaining that a whole lot of sheep went past that morning. He imitates the sound of a little lamb.

e150.description: Isabel declares herself a rooster with a shrill 'Cock-a-doodle-do!' Her red cheeks and bright eyes make her look like a rooster.

e151.description: Kezia suggests that Lottie be a donkey, arguing that she can't forget the 'Hee-haw' sound. Lottie accepts the role solemnly.

e152.description: Pip, as the bull, explains the card game rules to the other children. Players must match cards with the same number of spots and call out their animal sound when they match. Lottie struggles to understand the concept.

e153.description: Lottie expresses confusion about the game rules, asking if the matched cards are hers to keep. Pip becomes cross with her for not understanding.

e154.description: Kezia and Isabel encourage Lottie to play, with Isabel demonstrating how the game works. The other children recognize that Lottie is about to withdraw and hide.

e155.description: Pip gives Lottie his first card as a gift to encourage her to continue playing, demonstrating generosity and leadership.

e156.description: Lottie realizes she doesn't have a handkerchief for the game. Rags offers his very wet handkerchief, knotted together and containing a small starfish he is trying to tame. He warns her to use only one corner.

e157.description: Pip deals the cards quickly around the table while the children try unsuccessfully to see their cards. The children struggle to contain their excitement.

e158.description: Lottie timidly plays her first card, looking at it first to count the spots, despite Pip's instruction that she should turn it over without looking.

e159.description: The game proceeds with the children making their animal sounds. Pip as the bull charges over the table, Kezia as the bee makes a buzzing sound, Isabel as the rooster stands up and moves her elbows like wings.

e160.description: Pip as the bull makes a 'Mooe-ooo-er!' sound and charges over the table, seemingly eating the cards up.

e161.description: Kezia as the bee makes a 'Bss-ss!' sound during the game.

e162.description: Isabel as the rooster stands up in excitement and moves her elbows like wings while making a 'Cock-a-doodle-do!' sound.

e163.description: Rags as the sheep puts down the King of Diamonds and makes a 'Baa!' sound. Lottie puts down the King of Spain and has hardly any cards left.

e164.description: Lottie forgets what animal she is supposed to be, saying woefully 'I've forgotten what I am.' The other children encourage her to change roles.

e165.description: Lottie changes her role from donkey to dog, finding it much easier. She smiles again at the change.

e166.description: When Kezia and Lottie both have a matching card, Kezia waits on purpose to let Lottie play first. The other children make signs to Lottie and point. Lottie turns red and bewildered but finally calls out 'Hee-haw! Ke-zia.'

e167.description: Pip stops the game abruptly, holding up his hand and asking the others if they heard a knocking sound. He says he thought he heard 'a sort of knocking.'

e168.description: The children become mouse-still and listen intently for the mysterious sound. Kezia as the bee gives a shudder and asks why they shut the door, expressing fear.

e169.description: While the children were playing, the day faded and the gorgeous sunset blazed and died. The atmosphere in the washhouse shifts from playful to ominous.

e170.description: Quick dark comes racing over the sea, over the sand-hills, and up the paddock. The children become frightened to look in the corners of the washhouse, yet feel compelled to look with all their might.

e171.description: Somewhere far away, grandma is lighting a lamp. The blinds are being pulled down and the kitchen fire leaps in the tins on the mantelpiece, suggesting the household is settling in for the evening.

e172.description: Pip tells a frightening story about a giant spider as big as a saucer with long hairs like a gooseberry that could fall from the ceiling onto the table. He attributes the story to 'our Min' who supposedly saw such a spider.

e173.description: All the little heads jerk up and all the little bodies draw together and press together in fear after hearing Pip's spider story.

e174.description: Isabel as the rooster cries out 'Why doesn't somebody come and call us?' expressing the children's fear of abandonment. She reflects on the adults laughing and snug in the lamp-light, suggesting they have deliberately left the children alone.

e175.description: Isabel as the rooster asks why nobody comes to call them, expressing the children's anxiety about being forgotten or abandoned by the adults.

e176.description: The children realize that the adults have not forgotten them but have deliberately decided to leave them alone in the washhouse. This realization intensifies their fear and sense of abandonment.

e177.description: Lottie gives a piercing scream, causing all the other children to jump off the forms and scream as well. She shrieks 'A face—a face looking!'

e178.description: A pale face with black eyes and a black beard is pressed against the washhouse window. The children are terrified, believing they are seeing something supernatural or threatening.

e179.description: The children panic and cry out 'Grandma! Mother! Somebody!' in terror at the face in the window.

e180.description: The washhouse door opens before the children can reach it, revealing the source of the mysterious face.

e181.description: Uncle Jonathan is revealed to have come to take the little boys (Pip and Rags) home. The mysterious and terrifying face belongs to a family member, resolving the children's terror.

e182.description: Jonathan encounters Linda in the front garden where she is walking up and down, stopping to pick off dead flowers and tend to carnations. She wears a white frock and a yellow, pink-fringed shawl from the Chinaman's shop.

e183.description: Linda greets Jonathan with 'Hallo, Jonathan!' Jonathan responds by whipping off his shabby panama hat, pressing it against his breast, dropping on one knee, and kissing Linda's hand. He addresses her with theatrical language: 'Greeting, my Fair One! Greeting, my Celestial Peach Blossom!' and asks where the other women are.

e184.description: Linda explains that Beryl is out playing bridge and her mother is giving the boy his bath. Jonathan asks if he has come to borrow something. Linda drops into Beryl's hammock under the manuka tree, and Jonathan stretches himself on the grass beside her, pulling a long stalk and beginning to chew it. They settle into conversation as the sun begins to sink.

e185.description: Linda asks Jonathan if he is going back to the office on Monday. Jonathan responds with theatrical language about the 'cage door' opening and closing upon the 'victim' for another eleven months and a week.

e186.description: Linda responds that it must be awful, speaking slowly. Jonathan asks if she would have him laugh or weep. Linda replies vaguely that one gets used to anything, and Jonathan responds with a deep 'Hum' and wonders how it is done, saying he has never managed it.

e187.description: Linda observes Jonathan as he lies on the grass and reflects on his character. She notes that he is only an ordinary clerk, that Stanley earns twice as much money as he does, and wonders what is the matter with Jonathan. She concludes that he has no ambition.

e188.description: Linda reflects further on Jonathan's character, noting that he is gifted and exceptional, passionately fond of music, and always full of new ideas and schemes. However, nothing comes of his plans. She observes that the new fire blazes in Jonathan but quickly falls to ashes, leaving him with a look of hunger in his black eyes. At these times he exaggerates his manner of speaking and sings in church with fearful dramatic intensity.

e189.description: Jonathan expresses his deep dissatisfaction with office work, comparing it to being in jail. He elaborates on his metaphor of being an insect trapped in a room, dashing against walls and windows, thinking constantly of the shortness of life and the vast dangerous garden waiting outside, undiscovered and unexplored.

e190.description: Linda begins to ask why Jonathan doesn't leave, but Jonathan interrupts with an exultant 'Ah!' and poses the question back to her. He elaborates on why he doesn't escape, comparing himself again to an insect that cannot stop banging and flopping. He mentions his two boys to provide for but admits he could cut off to sea or get a job up-country. He then confesses in a changed voice that he is weak, has no stamina, no anchor, and no guiding principle. He begins to sing.

e191.description: The sun sets. In the western sky there are great masses of crushed-up rose-colored clouds. Broad beams of light shine through the clouds and beyond them. Overhead the blue fades and turns a pale gold, and the bush outlined against it gleams dark and brilliant like metal.

e192.description: Linda reflects on the sunset beams of light. She thinks of how they usually remind one of Jehovah, the jealous God, the Almighty, whose eye is upon you, and how at His coming the whole earth will shake into a ruined graveyard. But tonight it seems to Linda that there is something infinitely joyful and loving in those silver beams. The sea breathes softly as if it would draw that tender, joyful beauty into its own bosom.

e193.description: Jonathan's shadowy voice comes from the darkness, saying 'It's all wrong, it's all wrong' and complaining that the scene is not the setting for 'three stools, three desks, three inkpots and a wire blind.' Linda knows he will never change but asks if it is too late, even now.

e194.description: Jonathan intones that he is old, bends towards Linda, and passes his hand over his head. He tells her to look at his black hair, which is speckled all over with silver like the breast plumage of a black fowl.

e195.description: Linda is surprised to discover that Jonathan is grey. She had no idea that he was grey. As he stands up beside her and sighs and stretches, she sees him for the first time not resolute, not gallant, not careless, but touched already with age. He looks very tall on the darkening grass.

e196.description: A thought crosses Linda's mind as she observes Jonathan: 'He is like a weed.' This observation captures her sense of his tall, somewhat unkempt appearance and his rootless, drifting nature.

e197.description: Jonathan stoops again and kisses Linda's fingers. He murmurs 'Heaven reward thy sweet patience, lady mine' and says he must go seek his heirs to his fame and fortune. He departs.

e198.description: Light shines in the windows of the bungalow, casting square patches of gold on the pinks and peaked marigolds. Florrie the cat comes out onto the veranda and sits on the top step, her white paws close together and her tail curled round. She looks content, expressing relief that the long day is over.

e199.description: The rumble of the coach is heard, along with the crack of Kelly's whip. The coach comes near enough for one to hear the voices of men from town talking loudly together.

e200.description: The coach stops at the Burnells' gate.

e201.description: Stanley is half-way up the garden path when he sees Linda. He greets her, asking 'Is that you, darling?'

e202.description: Stanley leaps across the flower-bed and seizes Linda in his arms, enfolding her in a familiar, eager, strong embrace.

e203.description: Stanley stammers 'Forgive me, darling, forgive me' and puts his hand under Linda's chin to lift her face to him. Linda responds with amusement, asking 'Forgive you? But whatever for?'

e204.description: Stanley explains his distress, saying he has thought of nothing else all day and has had the hell of a day. He confesses he considered dashing out to telegraph Linda but worried the wire might not reach her before he did. He says he has been in tortures.

e205.description: Stanley reveals that he left without saying goodbye to Linda that morning and cannot imagine how he could have done such a thing. He blames his confounded temper and says he has suffered for it enough today. He takes Linda in his arms again.

e206.description: Linda asks Stanley what he has in his hand, asking if they are new gloves. Stanley humbly explains they are a cheap pair of wash-leather ones. He noticed Bell was wearing some in the coach that morning, so as he was passing a shop, he dashed in and got himself a pair.

e207.description: Linda pulls one of the large, pale gloves onto her own fingers and looks at her hand, turning it this way and that. She continues smiling.

e208.description: Stanley wants to say 'I was thinking of you the whole time I bought them,' and recognizes it is true, but for some reason he cannot say it.

e209.description: Stanley suggests they go inside. Linda continues smiling as they prepare to enter the house.

e210.description: Beryl experiences the thrill of being awake at night while everyone else sleeps, moving stealthily through her room and feeling like a conspirator. She feels more wakeful with each breath, entering a new, wonderful, thrilling world.

e211.description: Beryl's perception of her room transforms from ordinary and unnoticed during the day to suddenly dear, darling, and precious at night. She experiences joy in owning things and recognizes the room as hers.

e212.description: Beryl imagines two people in her room - a man holding her with his arms around his neck, whispering 'My beauty, my little beauty!' She dismisses this as nonsense and rubbish but sees it plainly in her mind.

e213.description: Beryl looks out her window at the moonlit garden where flowers, bushes, leaves, white palings, and stars all appear as conspirators in her romantic fantasy. The manuka tree appears bent like a bird on one leg stretching out a wing.

e214.description: Beryl's romantic fantasy fades as she contemplates the sadness of solitude. She realizes her deep loneliness despite having relations and friends, and recognizes her desperate need for a lover who will find and expect the true Beryl.

e215.description: Beryl recalls Mrs. Kember's voice encouraging her to enjoy herself while young, followed by her indifferent laugh. Beryl recognizes the fascination of having power over people, though she struggles with inexperience and fear of seeming stuffy.

e216.description: Beryl desperately wonders why 'he' doesn't come soon, fearing that if she continues living at the Bay, anything may happen to her. She expresses urgent longing for a lover's arrival.

e217.description: Beryl dismisses a mocking inner voice that questions whether 'he' is coming at all. She cannot accept the possibility that she might never marry, insisting that it is impossible for Beryl Fairfield, a lovely fascinating girl, to remain unmarried.
